name: Jade Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for speaking with me, Jade. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lettings negotiator at the Northgate branch of a regional chain, so I mostly rent out flats rather than sell them. A day is viewings for young professionals, checking tenants' references, chasing landlords to fix boilers, and a lot of email. I've been doing it about five years, and I'm decent, not a star.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like matching the right person to the right flat, like the nurse last month who needed somewhere near the hospital with a parking space. What wears me out is landlords who won't spend a penny and tenants who ring at nine at night about a leak. I live alone in a one-bed and pay rent myself, so I know both sides of that argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a few handy tools and that's it. I already use an AI writer now and then for property adverts, so I'd say it's a nice helper, nothing more. I'd probably say that in the branch WhatsApp group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means things stay as they are, and that's fine by me. Lettings is steady work, because people always need somewhere to rent. My pay is typical, my rent is manageable, and I've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and maybe use the AI writer a bit more for the boring listings. I'd keep putting a little away each month, and I'd go for the senior negotiator role when my manager Priya finally moves up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. It's a normal life with normal annoyances, like the landlord who still hasn't fixed flat 4B's window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your money or job that worries you, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not hugely. My rent went up eight percent this year, which stung, but I absorbed it. The branch is busy, so I don't think about losing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine tasks would the tools take off you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing adverts and maybe sorting viewing times. That saves me maybe an hour a day. I'd spend it on the phone with landlords, which is the bit that actually earns fees.

say: AI turned out to be **a handy helper** for adverts, nothing more.
Lettings stays **busy** because people always need somewhere to rent.
think: My job, **rent and savings** all feel steady enough.
The rent rise of **eight percent** stung but didn't sink me.
do: Use the **AI writer** a bit more for routine listings.
Keep **saving monthly** and aim for the senior negotiator role.
Spend the **saved hour** on calls with landlords.
feel: Calm, with only **everyday annoyances** like slow landlord repairs.
S0.quote: Lettings is steady work, because people always need somewhere to rent.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **now and then**, so the plateau barely touches her.
Her **lettings role** feels steadier to her than sales would.
She aims for **promotion** rather than any big change.

steps.text: Apply for senior negotiator when the role opens at Northgate
Use the AI writer for routine flat adverts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's changing how we work, and the agents who learn the new tools will be fine. That's the sensible line, and it's what head office would want us to say. I'd say it to my mum too, so she stops sending me news stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, lettings is almost all the stuff on your card. Referencing, booking viewings, writing tenancy agreements, answering tenant emails, all of it is thinking work. I think head office would merge Northgate with the town-centre branch and keep half of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do whatever AI training head office offers in the first month and get properly good at it, not just now and then. I'd push my savings from four months to six by cutting the gym and eating out. And I'd look at a property management course, because looking after buildings is harder to automate than paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not panicking, but it would be the first thing I think about every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the branch would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, who does our admin, because his whole job is the paperwork. And me, if I'm honest, because I'm average. The ones who'd stay are the top performers and the ones who know the landlords personally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you choose the course over waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work for someone else. If a couple of people from other branches did it and moved into block management, I'd sign up the next week. I don't jump first, but I don't like being last either.

say: Agents who **learn the tools** will be fine.
I'd say the **sensible line** at work and to my mum.
think: Most of lettings is **paperwork and email**, exactly what the card describes.
Head office could **merge branches** and keep half of us.
do: Take **head office's AI training** in the first month and master it.
Raise savings from four to **six months** by cutting the gym and eating out.
Look into a **property management** course once others have tried it.
feel: Anxious, with it being **first thing** on my mind each morning.
S1.quote: Lettings is almost all the stuff on your card. Referencing, booking viewings, writing tenancy agreements, answering tenant emails, all of it is thinking work.
fieldNote: She quickly saw that **lettings admin** is the core of what the card describes.
Her public line sounds **confident**, but privately she expects half the team to go.
She'd act once **others prove** the path, which fits her steady style.

steps.text: Finish head office's AI training in the first month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody could have prepared for this, and I'd mean it. I'd probably post something on LinkedIn about adapting, because everyone would be. Then I'd delete it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the lettings negotiator job mostly disappears by 2028. A tenant could find a flat, get referenced and sign a lease with an AI in an evening. The viewings and the inspections might last until the robots come around 2031, but that's a few people, not a whole branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd ask Priya if I could move into property inspections, the hands-on bit where you check flats at the start and end of a tenancy. I'd keep my savings untouched and move to a cheaper flat if my rent came up for renewal. I'd also look at what jobs the AI firms create around housing, if any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd feel like I'd done everything right and it didn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if your pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car finance, I'd hand the car back. Then the phone contract. Rent is the last thing I'd let slip, because I see what happens to tenants who fall behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep savings untouched, but also move flats. Isn't moving expensive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, the deposit and the van. But a cheaper flat saves me maybe two hundred a month, so it pays back in a few months. I'd rather spend once than bleed every month.

say: Nobody could have **prepared** for something this fast, and I'd mean it.
I'd post something about **adapting** on LinkedIn like everyone else, then delete it.
think: The **lettings negotiator** job mostly disappears by 2028.
Only **viewings and inspections** last until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Ask Priya to move me into **property inspections** within months.
Move to a **cheaper flat** at renewal to save about £200 a month.
Hand back the **car on finance** if my pay stops.
feel: Frightened, like I'd **done everything right** and it didn't matter.
S2.quote: A tenant could find a flat, get referenced and sign a lease with an AI in an evening.
fieldNote: She expects **her job to go**, with inspections as a short bridge.
She knows how **falling behind on rent** goes, so rent is the last bill to slip.
Her feeling of **unfairness** was stronger than any blame aimed at anyone.

steps.text: Ask Priya (her manager) to move her into flat inspections
Move to a cheaper flat when the lease is up
Hand back the car on finance if pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to get ready, so let's use them. I'd probably start a chat with the other negotiators about what we're each planning. Somebody has to say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me to get out of the paperwork side before 2031. If I'm in inspections or block management by then, I've got until about 2034 before robots matter. That's not forever, but it's a career's worth of breathing room for someone my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the property management qualification over the next eighteen months, evenings and online. I'd keep using AI at work more each year so I'm not behind. And I'd save hard to keep six months in the bank, because changing jobs at twenty-nine might mean a pay dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable, but I feel like I've got a plan, which helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm moving from renting flats out to looking after buildings, and that it's still property. She'd worry anyway, she always does. But she'd like that it has a qualification at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you give up the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If block management got automated just as fast. I'd watch what happens to the managing agents in the first couple of years. If they're cutting too, I'd rethink.

say: We've got **a few years**, so let's use them.
I'd start a **group chat** with negotiators about everyone's plans.
think: Five years is enough to leave **the paperwork side** before 2031.
Moving into **building management** buys time until about 2034.
do: Finish a **property management qualification** within eighteen months.
Use **AI at work** more each year so I'm not behind.
Keep **six months saved** to cover a pay dip when switching.
feel: Uncomfortable, but steadier because I have **a plan**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to get out of the paperwork side before 2031.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her from **frightened to planning**.

steps.text: Study for a property management qualification over eighteen months
Use the agency's AI tools for more of each day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if you're sensible. I'd tell younger agents not to panic but not to coast either. That's how I'd put it at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still change career, just at my own pace. I'd probably give it three or four years, watch who moves first, then follow the ones it works for. By 2036 I'd want to be in something with a lot of face-to-face and hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in lettings for now and go for the senior negotiator job, because a better title helps whatever comes next. Around 2029 I'd start the property management course. I'd keep using AI tools as they come in and keep saving steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. It's like knowing your lease ends in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch who moves first. Who are you watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, my manager, and a friend from college who went into building surveying. If my friend's doing well in three years, that's a strong sign. I trust people I know more than headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change anything in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd try to buy a flat sooner rather than later, while my income is steady. I don't love owning, but I've seen enough landlords put rents up to know I'd rather not rent at fifty.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** to get ready if you're sensible.
I'd tell younger agents at work not to **panic or coast**.
think: I'd still **change career**, just at my own pace.
By 2036 I want work with **face-to-face** and hands-on parts.
do: Go for the **senior negotiator** job while staying in lettings.
Look at **buying a flat** sooner while income is steady.
feel: Uneasy, like knowing **a lease ends** in ten years.
S4.quote: I've seen enough landlords put rents up to know I'd rather not rent at fifty.
fieldNote: With ten years she'd **follow others** who change first.
She uses a **college friend** in surveying as her test case.

steps.text: Apply for the senior negotiator job at Northgate
Start the property management course around 2029
Save a deposit to buy a flat in the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out of a job before I'd finished any course. What would help is head office telling us early and paying for retraining, and maybe a scheme where agents can move into property management with a year of training on full pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about tenants. If lots of people lose jobs, rents get missed, and my job gets uglier before it disappears. I'd be the one ringing people who can't pay.
